chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, from Jarrah Al-Madaini, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he

forbade from what intoxicates from the drinks, all of it, and forbade the date husk and the pumpkin Nabidh, and he said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whatever a lot of it intoxicates, a little of it is forbidden.'

key_terms.النَّقِيرَ: A specific type of drink made from date husks
key_terms.نَبِيذَ: Nabidh, a fermented drink made by soaking dates or grapes in water

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on small amounts of intoxicating drinks in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of 'kathir wa qalil' (much and little) in Shia jurisprudence, clarifying that the prohibition of khamr (intoxicants) applies to both large and small quantities once the intoxicating effect is present. By specifically mentioning 'an-Naqir' and 'Nabidh al-Dubba', the Imam highlights the historical context of pre-Islamic and early Islamic fermentation practices, ensuring that common local beverages were not exempted from the general rule. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the substance's effect rather than just its source, reinforcing the complete prohibition of all intoxicants.
